parsed.explanation: Formal gender-identity protections exist but enforcement is weak. The operative regime exposes visitors to document/appearance mismatch in services and, if arrested or detained, to birth-sex custodial isolation, strip searches, misgendering and refused protection, with no working remedy. Society shows commonplace discrimination and violence, hate speech and impunity, though Pride is public and some court/Equality Council interventions occurred. No routine border or visitor-specific criminal targeting is documented. The combination of tier-one custody exposure, hostile social climate and ineffective remedies places risk in the lower Elevated band.

entry_documents.exposure: Documented trans woman denied bank service over document/appearance mismatch; visitors could face similar ID checks.
entry_documents.protection: No criminal document law; Equality Council confirmed discrimination and recommended measures.
entry_documents.interaction: Mismatch at services or checks may escalate to questioning or refusal; implementation unknown.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Trans man placed in men’s isolation unit, refused protection unit, forced strip searches, bathroom intrusion, misgendering; recent.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Ombudsman and LGBT group notified; no effective remedy documented.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Any arrest/detention could produce tier-one custodial humiliation.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Occupied region prohibits promotion of non-traditional relations; enforcement unsourced.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Local propaganda bans were struck down; no current visitor facility ban documented elsewhere.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Travel into the occupied region could add restrictive law; national facilities lack explicit rules.

care_services.exposure: No documented visitor care denial; only general discrimination common.
care_services.interaction: Clinic encounters could expose mismatch or stigma; unresolved.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Hate speech serious, politicians derogatory, discrimination common, impunity; prison staff humiliation.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Gender identity is in anti-discrimination and hate-crime law; courts invalidated some local bans.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Paper protections are discounted by poor enforcement.

minors_guardians.exposure: No documented age-dependent custody, facility or guardian restrictions for visitors with minors.
minors_guardians.interaction: Minor would share general exposure; care/school/detention unknowns.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Discrimination and violence described as commonplace; Pride earlier attacked or cancelled; arson complaint refused.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Police protected 2018 Pride; 2024 Pride proceeded; Equality Council acted once.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Protection is inconsistent; reporting may worsen exposure.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Equality Council measure unimplemented; prison claims denied; occupied-region enforcement unknown.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Formal courts, ombudsman and equality body exist.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Remedies rarely work quickly for short-stay visitors.

anchor_checks.comparison: Ours is higher than 0.35-B: no documented routine passport seizures or street identity checks for visitors. It is lower in custody severity, but Pride’s public progress and formal equality findings offset some risk, putting it above the purely 0.35 visitor-stop pattern.

Closest to 0.45-A: document/appearance mismatch produces service refusal and weak remedies. Ours is slightly lower because the prison case shows state-tolerated isolation and staff humiliation, while 0.45-A lacks comparable tier-one custody harm.

Lower than 0.55-B: no documented secondary screening or refusal, but custody exposure and commonplace violence are more severe than administrative border delay. Ours is not 0.55 because remedy failure and prison humiliation dominate.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime mixes nominal legal recognition with weak enforcement and hostile social practice. The key visitor-facing harms are document/appearance mismatch in ordinary services and, more severely, custodial placement, isolation, strip searches and misgendering when a traveller interacts with police or prisons. Pride’s public progress and some Equality Council or court interventions prevent the rating from falling into High Risk, but they do not offset unremedied state custody practices or commonplace prejudice. Occupied-region law and minor-specific exposures remain uncertain. Combined, this is lower Elevated Risk.
